result:
Neither. The premise is the problem: more agents don't always give better results.

Think of a group project. Five people can beat one person on a big job. But every extra person adds meetings, handoffs and a chance that two people misread each other. Past a point, the coordination costs more than the work it saves.

Agents behave the same way. Each one is its own loop of model calls (you've traced that loop already). Each call re-reads its instructions and context, and you pay for every token. Every handoff between agents is also a place where details get lost. If the booking agent tells the manuals agent "the laser cutter," and the student actually asked about the large-format one, that detail is gone. Ten agents means more calls, more tokens and more handoffs than five. With your small budget, that is a real cost.

Splitting tends to pay off in two cases:
- **The work is big and can run in parallel**, like researching ten separate machines at once.
- **One agent's context gets overloaded**, with too many tools or too much text for it to choose well.

Your assistant is three tasks: answer from manuals, check the calendar, book time. Those are mostly sequential and small, so a single agent with three well-described tools is the sensible starting point. Parts with a fixed order, such as "check availability, then book," may not need an agent at all. They can be a plain workflow. Only split when you can point to a specific failure that splitting would fix.

So the question to bring to your design review is "what problem does a second agent solve that one agent with good tools doesn't?"

Quick check: for the request "Book the 3D printer for Friday at 2," would you give the booking step its own agent? Say why or why not.

I can teach this properly as a lesson on workflows versus agents and multi-agent systems. First, though, context and memory is next in your plan, if you'd like that one instead.
